claim: The Gillespie algorithm is commonly used to simulate and analyze complex chemical reaction networks.
source: The Gillespie algorithm is commonly used to simulate and analyze complex chemical reaction networks.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the Gillespie algorithm's usage.

claim: The differentiable Gillespie algorithm (DGA) approximates discontinuous operations in the exact Gillespie algorithm using smooth functions.
source: The differentiable Gillespie algorithm (DGA) approximates discontinuous operations in the exact Gillespie algorithm using smooth functions, allowing for the calculation of gradients using backpropagation.
evidence: This is the core methodological claim stated in the abstract describing how the DGA works.

claim: The DGA allows for the calculation of gradients using backpropagation.
source: The differentiable Gillespie algorithm (DGA) approximates discontinuous operations in the exact Gillespie algorithm using smooth functions, allowing for the calculation of gradients using backpropagation.
evidence: This is stated as a direct consequence of the smooth function approximations in the DGA.

claim: The DGA can be used to quickly and accurately learn kinetic parameters using gradient descent.
source: The DGA can be used to quickly and accurately learn kinetic parameters using gradient descent and design biochemical networks with desired properties.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the DGA in the abstract.

claim: The DGA can be used to design biochemical networks with desired properties.
source: The DGA can be used to quickly and accurately learn kinetic parameters using gradient descent and design biochemical networks with desired properties.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the DGA in the abstract.

claim: The DGA can successfully learn kinetic parameters from experimental measurements of mRNA expression levels from two distinct Escherichia coli promoters.
source: We show that the DGA can be used to: (1) successfully learn kinetic parameters from experimental measurements of mRNA expression levels from two distinct Escherichia coli promoters
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated result in the abstract.

claim: The DGA can design nonequilibrium promoter architectures with desired input–output relationships.
source: (2) design nonequilibrium promoter architectures with desired input–output relationships.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated result in the abstract.

claim: Randomness is a defining feature of our world.
source: Randomness is a defining feature of our world.
evidence: This is a general statement made in the introduction.

claim: Stock market fluctuations, the movement of particles in fluids, and the change of allele frequencies in organismal populations can all be described using the language of stochastic processes.
source: Stock market fluctuations, the movement of particles in fluids, and even the change of allele frequencies in organismal populations can all be described using the language of stochastic processes.
evidence: This is stated as examples of stochastic processes in the introduction.

claim: Disciplines as diverse as physics, biology, ecology, evolution, finance, and engineering have all developed tools to mathematically model stochastic processes.
source: For this reason, disciplines as diverse as physics, biology, ecology, evolution, finance, and engineering have all developed tools to mathematically model stochastic processes (Van Kampen, 1992; Gardiner, 2009; Rolski et al., 2009; Wong and Hajek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: An especially fruitful area of research has been the study of stochastic gene expression in single cells.
source: In the context of biology, an especially fruitful area of research has been the study of stochastic gene expression in single cells (McAdams and Arkin, 1997; Elowitz et al., 2002; Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008; Sanchez and Golding, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The small number of molecules involved in gene expression make stochasticity an inherent feature of protein production.
source: The small number of molecules involved in gene expression make stochasticity an inherent feature of protein production and numerous mathematical and computational techniques have been developed to model gene expression and relate mathematical models to experimental observations (Paulsson, 2005; Wilkinson, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about gene expression with supporting citations.

claim: The Gillespie algorithm is an extremely efficient computational technique used to simulate the time evolution of a system in which events occur randomly and discretely.
source: The Gillespie algorithm is an extremely efficient computational technique used to simulate the time evolution of a system in which events occur randomly and discretely (Gillespie, 1977).
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the Gillespie algorithm with citation.

claim: The Gillespie algorithm is widely employed across numerous disciplines including epidemiology, ecology, neuroscience, and chemical kinetics.
source: Beyond gene expression, the Gillespie algorithm is widely employed across numerous disciplines to model stochastic systems characterized by discrete, randomly occurring events including epidemiology (Pineda-Krch, 2008), ecology (Parker and Kamenev, 2009; Dobramysl et al., 2018), neuroscience (Benayoun et al., 2010; Rijal et al., 2024), and chemical kinetics (Gillespie, 1976; Gillespie, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature in multiple fields.

claim: The DGA modifies the traditional Gillespie algorithm to take advantage of powerful automatic differentiation libraries.
source: The DGA modifies the traditional Gillespie algorithm to take advantage of powerful automatic differentiation libraries for example, PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019), Jax (Bradbury et al., 2018), and Julia (Bezanson et al., 2017) and gradient-based optimization.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the DGA with citations to the relevant libraries.

claim: The DGA allows us to quickly fit kinetic parameters to data and design discrete stochastic systems with a desired behavior.
source: The DGA allows us to quickly fit kinetic parameters to data and design discrete stochastic systems with a desired behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the DGA.

claim: In the traditional Gillespie algorithm both the selection of the index for the next reaction and the updates of chemical species are both discontinuous functions of the kinetic parameters.
source: As shown in Figure 1, in the traditional Gillespie algorithm both the selection of the index for the next reaction and the updates of chemical species are both discontinuous functions of the kinetic parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The DGA modifies the traditional Gillespie algorithm by approximating discrete operations with continuous, differentiable functions.
source: To circumnavigate these difficulties, the DGA modifies the traditional Gillespie algorithm by approximating discrete operations with continuous, differentiable functions, smoothing out abrupt transitions to facilitate gradient computation via automatic differentiation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The DGA preserves the core characteristics of the original Gillespie algorithm while enabling integration with modern deep learning techniques.
source: This significant modification preserves the core characteristics of the original algorithm while enabling integration with modern deep learning techniques.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the DGA.

claim: Jones et al., 2014 independently measured the kinetic parameters for promoter architectures using orthogonal experiments.
source: An especially appealing aspect of Jones et al., 2014 is that the authors independently measured the kinetic parameters for these promoter architectures using orthogonal experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the Jones et al. 2014 study.

claim: The DGA is no longer exact, unlike the Gillespie algorithm.
source: The foremost of these is that unlike the Gillespie algorithm, the DGA is no longer exact.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the DGA.

claim: The DGA replaces the exact discrete stochastic system by an approximate differentiable stochastic system.
source: The DGA replaces the exact discrete stochastic system by an approximate differentiable stochastic system.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the approximations in the DGA.

claim: The effect of the approximations introduced by the DGA may be pronounced in complex settings such as the calculation of rare events, modeling of tail-driven processes, or dealing with non-stationary time series.
source: However, we note that the effect of the approximations introduced by the DGA may be pronounced in more complex settings such as the calculation of rare events, modeling of tail-driven processes, or dealing with non-stationary time series.
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation of the DGA.

claim: The DGA can accurately replicate the results of the exact Gillespie simulation for steady-state mRNA distributions.
source: Figure 4a compares the probability distribution function (PDF) for the steady-state mRNA levels obtained from the DGA (in red) and the exact Gillespie simulation (in blue). The close overlap of these distributions demonstrates that the DGA can accurately replicate the results of the exact Gillespie simulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The DGA fails to accurately capture the tails of the underlying PDF.
source: As observed in Figure 4a, the DGA also fails to accurately capture the tails of the underlying PDF.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4a.

claim: The discrepancy in capturing tails arises because rare events result from very frequent low-probability reaction events where the sigmoid approximation used in the DGA significantly impacts the reaction selection process.
source: This discrepancy arises because rare events result from very frequent low-probability reaction events where the sigmoid approximation used in the DGA significantly impacts the reaction selection process and, consequently, the final simulation results.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the tail discrepancy.

claim: The DGA's approximation introduces only a 0.3% deviation from the exact distribution, relative to the total uncertainty (entropy) in the exact system.
source: In percentage terms, this ratio represents a 0.3% divergence, meaning that the DGA's approximation introduces only a 0.3% deviation from the exact distribution, relative to the total uncertainty (entropy) in the exact system.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the JSD/H ratio.

claim: The differentiable Gillespie overestimates the probability of being in the 'OFF' state and underestimates the probability of being in the 'ON' state.
source: The differentiable Gillespie overestimates the probability of being in the 'OFF' state and underestimates the probability of being in the 'ON' state.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Despite errors, the DGA does a reasonable job of matching the results of the exact simulations for discrete systems.
source: Nonetheless, given the discrete nature of this system, the DGA does a reasonable job of matching the results of the exact simulations.
evidence: This is stated as an overall assessment of the DGA's performance.

claim: Despite errors, the DGA is able to accurately capture gradient information and works remarkably well at gradient-based optimization of loss functions.
source: As we will see below, despite these errors the DGA is able to accurately capture gradient information and hence works remarkably well at gradient-based optimization of loss functions.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding that will be demonstrated.

claim: Two-state promoter systems are commonly studied because they provide a simplified yet powerful model for understanding gene regulation dynamics.
source: Two-state promoter systems are commonly studied because they provide a simplified yet powerful model for understanding gene regulation dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for studying two-state promoters.

claim: For the two-state promoter model, both mean mRNA expression and the Fano factor can be calculated analytically.
source: An appealing feature of this model is that both mean mRNA expression and the Fano factor can be calculated analytically and there exist beautiful quantitative measurements of both these quantities (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the two-state promoter model.

claim: There exist quantitative measurements of mean mRNA expression and Fano factor for two-state promoters.
source: An appealing feature of this model is that both mean mRNA expression and the Fano factor can be calculated analytically and there exist beautiful quantitative measurements of both these quantities (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The loss function around the true parameters is quite flat.
source: As can be seen, the loss function around the true parameters is quite flat and the learned parameters live at the edge of this flat region.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b and stated in the text.

claim: The flatness of the loss function reflects the fact that the mean and standard deviation of the mRNA distribution depend weakly on the kinetic parameters.
source: The flatness of the loss function reflects the fact that the mean and standard deviation of the mRNA distribution depend weakly on the kinetic parameters.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the flat loss function.

claim: When all three parameters k_on^R, r, and γ are unknown, there are many sets of parameters that all minimize the loss function.
source: As discussed above, in this case, there are many sets of parameters that all minimize the loss function in Equation 11.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the degenerate case.

claim: Though the true parameters and learned parameter values differ significantly in the degenerate case, they do so along 'sloppy' directions where loss function is flat.
source: As can be seen in the plots, though the true parameters and learned parameter values differ significantly, they do so along 'sloppy' directions where loss function is flat.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b and stated in the text.

claim: Jones et al., 2014 measured how mRNA expression changes in a system well described by the two-state gene expression model.
source: To test the DGA in this more difficult setting, we reanalyze experiments by Jones et al., 2014 which measured how mRNA expression changes in a system well described by the two-state gene expression model in Figure 3.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the Jones et al. 2014 experiments.

claim: The learned parameter values indicate that mRNA transcription occurs much faster compared to the unbinding of the repressor.
source: These values indicate that mRNA transcription occurs much faster compared to the unbinding of the repressor, suggesting that once the promoter is in an active state, it produces mRNA rapidly.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the learned parameters.

claim: The relatively high mRNA degradation rates indicate a mechanism for fine-tuning gene expression levels.
source: The relatively high mRNA degradation rates indicate a mechanism for fine-tuning gene expression levels, ensuring that mRNA does not persist too long in the cell, which could otherwise lead to prolonged expression even after promoter deactivation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the learned parameters.

claim: The repressor binding rates decrease with the mean mRNA level.
source: As expected, the repressor binding rates decrease with the mean mRNA level (see Figure 7c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c and stated in the text.

claim: For the lacUD5 promoter, the mean percentage error for predictions of the Fano factor is 25%.
source: We find that for the lacUD5 and the 5DL1 promoters, the mean percentage errors for predictions of the Fano factor are 25% and 28%, respectively (see Appendix 6).
evidence: This is stated as a quantification of the prediction error.

claim: For the 5DL1 promoter, the mean percentage error for predictions of the Fano factor is 28%.
source: We find that for the lacUD5 and the 5DL1 promoters, the mean percentage errors for predictions of the Fano factor are 25% and 28%, respectively (see Appendix 6).
evidence: This is stated as a quantification of the prediction error.

claim: The predictions of the DGA for r/γ agree remarkably well with ground truth measurements for both the lacUD5 and 5DL1 promoters.
source: In Figure 7b, the predictions of the DGA agree remarkably well for both the lacUD5 and 5DL1 promoters.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b and stated in the text.

claim: The four-state promoter model allows for nonequilibrium currents, unlike the two-state promoter model.
source: We have chosen this more complex promoter architecture because, unlike the two-state promoter model analyzed above, it allows for nonequilibrium currents.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for choosing the four-state model.

claim: Recent works have investigated how cells can tune kinetic parameters to operate out of equilibrium in order to achieve increased sharpness/sensitivity.
source: In making this choice, we are inspired by numerous recent works have investigated how cells can tune kinetic parameters to operate out of equilibrium in order to achieve increased sharpness/sensitivity (Nicholson and Gingrich, 2023Lammers et al., 2023; Zoller et al., 2022; Wong and Gunawardena, 2020; Dixit et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: There is good agreement between the desired and learned input-output relations for the four-state promoter model.
source: Figure 8b shows a comparison between the desired and learned input–output relations. This is good agreement between the learned and desired responses, showing that the DGA is able to design dose–response curves with different sensitivities and maximal values.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8b and stated in the text.

claim: Creating nonequilibrium kinetics represents a general design principle for engineering sharp responses.
source: This observation is consistent with recent works suggesting that creating such nonequilibrium kinetics represents a general design principle for engineering sharp responses (Lammers et al., 2023; Zoller et al., 2022; Wong and Gunawardena, 2020; Dixit et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The sharper response curve is achieved by consuming more energy.
source: Figure 8d shows a comparison between energy consumption and sharpness of the two learned circuits. Consistent with the results of Lammers et al., 2023, we find that the sharper response curve is achieved by consuming more energy.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8d and stated in the text.

claim: The DGA facilitates the use of gradient-based optimization techniques for parameter estimation and network design.
source: By integrating differentiable components into the traditional Gillespie algorithm, the DGA facilitates the use of gradient-based optimization techniques, such as gradient descent, for parameter estimation and network design.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the DGA in the discussion.

claim: The ability to smoothly approximate the discrete operations of the traditional Gillespie algorithm with continuous functions facilitates the computation of gradients via both forward- and reverse-mode automatic differentiation.
source: The ability to smoothly approximate the discrete operations of the traditional Gillespie algorithm with continuous functions facilitates the computation of gradients via both forward- and reverse-mode automatic differentiation, foundational techniques in machine learning, and has the potential to significantly expand the utility of stochastic simulations.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the DGA in the discussion.

claim: The DGA could accurately approximate the moments of the steady-state distribution and other major qualitative features.
source: We found the DGA could accurately approximate the moments of the steady-state distribution and other major qualitative features.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the benchmarking results.

claim: The DGA was less accurate at capturing information about the tails of distributions.
source: Unsurprisingly, it was less accurate at capturing information about the tails of distributions.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation observed in the benchmarking.

claim: The DGA could be accurately used for parameter estimation on both simulated and real experimental data.
source: We then demonstrated that the DGA could be accurately used for parameter estimation on both simulated and real experimental data.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the parameter estimation results.

claim: The capability to infer kinetic parameters from noisy experimental data underscores the robustness of the DGA.
source: This capability to infer kinetic parameters from noisy experimental data underscores the robustness of the DGA, making it a potentially powerful computation tool for real-world applications in quantitative biology.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the parameter estimation results.

claim: The DGA can be used to rapidly design complex biological systems with specific behaviors.
source: This demonstrates how the DGA can be used to rapidly design complex biological systems with specific behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the circuit design results.

claim: Computational design of synthetic circuits with differentiable simulations is expected to become an increasingly important tool in synthetic biology.
source: We expect computational design of synthetic circuits with differentiable simulations to become an increasingly important tool in synthetic biology.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction about the future impact of the DGA.

claim: How to adopt the DGA to utilize dynamical data remains an extremely important open question.
source: However, a powerful aspect of the traditional Gillespie algorithm is that it can be used to simulate dynamical trajectories. How to adopt the DGA to utilize dynamical data remains an extremely important open question.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and future direction.

claim: It will be interesting to see if the DGA can be adapted to understand the kinetic of rare events.
source: In addition, it will be interesting to see if the DGA can be adapted to understand the kinetic of rare events.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction.

claim: It will be interesting to compare the DGA with other recently developed approximation methods such as those based on tensor networks.
source: It will also be interesting to compare the DGA with other recently developed approximation methods such as those based on tensor networks (Strand et al., 2022; Nicholson and Gingrich, 2023).
evidence: This is stated as a future direction with citations.

claim: Extending the DGA to handle larger and more diverse datasets will be crucial for applications in epidemiology, evolution, ecology, and neuroscience.
source: Beyond the gene regulatory networks, extending the DGA to handle larger and more diverse datasets will be crucial for applications in epidemiology, evolution, ecology, and neuroscience.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction.

claim: The DGA could be extended to stochastic spatial systems by incorporating reaction–diffusion master equations or lattice-based models.
source: The DGA could also be extended to stochastic spatial systems by incorporating reaction–diffusion master equations or lattice-based models.
evidence: This is stated as a potential extension.

claim: The DGA's differentiability may enable efficient optimization of spatially heterogeneous reaction parameters.
source: Its differentiability may enable efficient optimization of spatially heterogeneous reaction parameters.
evidence: This is stated as a potential benefit of extending the DGA to spatial systems.

claim: Extensions of the DGA to spatial systems may need to address computational scalability and stability in high-dimensional spaces.
source: However, such extensions may need to address computational scalability and stability in high-dimensional spaces, especially in processes such as diffusion-driven pattern formation or spatial gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated as a potential challenge for spatial extensions.
